summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs for Mariner's chat assistant use case. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, workload sizing (QPS, concurrency), measurement plan including synthetic vs real traffic, warm vs cold cache considerations, and timeline for benchmark runs.
topics: Benchmark plan: synthetic loads & real traffic sampling
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to 45 minutes. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE on the account, and Priya from our SE team will lead the technical bit. Alicia, Marcus, Dana, thanks for making time. quick check - is this time still good?
[00:08] Alicia (Mariner): Yep good for me, thanks.
[00:11] Marcus (Mariner SRE): good here.
[00:13] Dana (Product): yep.
[00:15] Priya (Redwood SE): great, I'll jump into the SLO discussion — want to make sure we define success criteria clearly: TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99, and how we'll measure.
[00:25] Alicia: high level — our priority is chat latency for clinicians using the assistant. They need the first response quick so TTFT matters, but sustained throughput matters too for long synthesis tasks. We generally aim for interactive feel.
[00:38] Jordan: perfect. Can you quantify what interactive means for you — like acceptable delays?
[00:42] Alicia: ideally <200ms for the initial token in most cases, p95. p99 we'd like under 400ms. For token generation steady-state (TPOT) we'd like ~10-15ms p95 per token, p99 <30ms. But that's a rough starting point, we don't know feasibility across models/hardware.
[01:05] Priya: good, those are concrete. quick definitions to make sure we align: TTFT (time-to-first-token) = request timestamp to first token emitted, important for perceived latency in chat. TPOT (time-per-token) = average time between successive tokens once streaming starts; it's a proxy for throughput and smoothness for long outputs. Sometimes folks call TPOT 'per-token latency' or throughput token rate (tps).
[01:28] Marcus: just to clarify, are we measuring TTFT from client side or from gateway? we have network hops and potential VPC peering.
[01:33] Priya: good question — measurement plan should include both client-observed and server-side measurements. For the POC we'll provide a runbook that includes client-side synthetic tests (to capture real network), and server-side metrics (from Redwood: request receive timestamp, first-token timestamp, last-token timestamp, CPU/GPU utilization). we'll correlate traces.
[01:52] Dana: any gotchas? e.g., cache/warm vs cold starts.
[01:56] Priya: yes. KV/prefix cache and model warm caches change TTFT dramatically. We'll run three types of benchmarks: 1) cold-start scenarios (fresh worker, empty KV), 2) warm-run with prefix caching enabled, and 3) representative production traffic replay (using your sample dataset) to capture realistic patterns. We'll flag where caching skews numbers.
[02:20] Alicia: sounds good. For target quantiles, can Redwood measure p95 and p99 across all these scenarios? we want both.
[02:26] Priya: yes, we'll capture p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT and also report throughput in tokens/sec and QPS at different concurrency points.
[02:35] Jordan: let's talk numbers and sizing — Alicia, Marcus, what's current expected peak QPS and concurrency?
[02:42] Alicia: peak concurrent clinicians ~120 during peak shifts but actual chat QPS is lower because most sessions are short; average QPS target for POC let's assume 60 QPS with spikes to 200 QPS for short bursts. Token lengths vary — typical prompts are 80-200 tokens, some long summaries up to 1.5k tokens.
[03:05] Marcus: our infra ops want to know sustained tokens/sec per GPU for planning. any rule of thumb?
[03:10] Priya: depends on model and quantization. For a 2B-ish model on A100-ish hardware you'll see different TPOT than 13B quantized. We'll run recommended model variant profiling. For the booking POC we recommend testing 3 model profiles: a small fast model (e.g., 3B quantized), a mid-sized (13B quantized), and a high quality (70B or hosted equivalent) so you can pick the right latency/cost point.
[03:36] Jordan: also want to capture burst behavior — autoscaling and queueing effects. Priya, for the benchmark runbook, can you include steady-state ramp, spike test, and sustained long-run (30-60 min) to see tail metrics?
[03:47] Priya: yes. Proposed plan in the runbook:
 - Ramp test: linear ramp from 1 to target QPS over 10 minutes
 - Spike test: sudden jump to 2-3x peak for 2-5 minutes to validate autoscale/fallback
 - Sustained run: hold target QPS for 60 minutes to observe thermal behavior and tail latency
 - Payload matrix: prompt lengths 80, 250, 1000 tokens, streaming enabled
[04:10] Alicia: perfect. For SLOs, are the p95/p99 budgets per request or per token? we prefer per-request for user-visible SLOs.
[04:19] Priya: we can report both. Per-request TTFT p95/p99 is the UX metric. TPOT is more useful for capacity planning and cost. We'll map both to cost and error budgets. Example SLO set we discussed earlier: TTFT p95 < 200ms p99 < 450ms; TPOT p95 < 15ms p99 < 35ms for mid model. Those will be adjustable after profiling.
[04:44] Marcus: those TTFT numbers are aggressive depending on routing and VPC peering. Also encryption/KMS handshake can add overhead for Private deployments.
[04:52] Priya: noted — we'll include measurement slices: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private network path. For Private we instrument additional network hops and estimate added latency.
[05:02] Dana: what about cold token generation when model loads weights off disk? do we test model load time?
[05:07] Priya: yes cold-start includes process and model load. We'll run cold-start tests and capture time-to-ready per worker. Also measure resumed warm state (worker staying alive but kv cache empty). We'll timestamp all these.
[05:20] Alicia: how do you handle sampling for p99 — do you run long enough?
[05:24] Priya: p99 needs long-run or controlled adversarial spikes. Our suggested approach: run sustained 60 min tests and collect request-level metrics; for p99 we also run background noise and small retries to capture tail behavior; we log every request.
[05:38] Jordan: let's cover instrumentation and logging — what will Redwood provide?
[05:44] Priya: we'll provide a benchmark runbook, load scripts (k6/locust examples), an S3 bucket to push raw request logs if you want, and Grafana dashboards we preconfigure for TTFT/TPOT/p95/p99, token/sec, GPU util, and queue lengths. We'll also provide a sample harness for client-side synthetic measurements so you can run from your VPC.
[06:04] Marcus: can we correlate trace IDs back to Mariner's frontend? we need to reconcile traces for debugging.
[06:09] Priya: yes we support passing X-Request-ID or custom trace id and will include that in logs for correlation. We'll include example headers in runbook.
[06:18] Alicia: timeline — when can we start?
[06:23] Jordan: Jordan: we can kick off as soon as you share dataset and QPS targets. Proposed schedule: runbook and pricing sent by 2027-08-25, benchmark kickoff 2027-08-29, initial profiling results 2027-09-02, final bench summary 2027-09-06. does that work?
[06:38] Alicia: yes that works.
[06:40] Marcus: one more thing — security/compliance: we need to validate SOC2 and data residency. will you send security docs?
[06:47] Jordan: yes I'll send security pack and SOC2 report. Also include options for Private deployment if you need data not to leave your VPC.
[06:55] Dana: for acceptance criteria, what's the success definition for the POC?
[06:59] Priya: good to capture — proposed success criteria: 1) Meet TTFT p95/p99 targets for representative workload on chosen model profile in at least one deployment mode (Hosted or Dedicated) 2) Throughput capacity: demonstrate sustained target QPS with <x% error rate (we'll set x at 1% initially) 3) Operational metrics: end-to-end tracing in place and reproducible runbook 4) Cost estimate within expected budget (Jordan will provide cost per 1M tokens for each config).
[07:25] Alicia: makes sense; we'll sign off if TTFT/TPOT performance matches target and the operational runbook is solid.
[07:31] Jordan: ok. Quick question about model variants and fallbacks: if the chosen large model misses SLOs, would Redwood recommend fallback to a smaller model for degraded performance?
[07:40] Priya: yes — part of the POC we'll evaluate fallback policies and automated routing by latency/cost. We'll show how to route to lower-latency variants for tail mitigation. We'll also show quantization tradeoffs.
[07:53] Marcus: about measurement noise — where do we set concurrency per worker to simulate real users?
[07:58] Priya: we'll use a concurrency matrix: 1, 5, 10 concurrent streams per client to simulate single-user and multiplexed sessions, and measure per-request TTFT and aggregated throughput.
[08:10] Dana: do you have standard thresholds you recommend for clinician-facing apps?
[08:14] Priya: yes for chat UX many customers aim for TTFT p95 < 200-300ms. For TPOT p95 < 10-20ms depending on model. But it varies by model size and hardware. We'll produce a capability matrix after profiling.
[08:29] Jordan: let's capture final recap and next steps. We'll: 1) Priya shares runbook and load scripts by 2027-08-27; 2) Jordan shares pricing and legal pilot template by 2027-08-25; 3) Mariner shares dataset + traffic profile + network diagram by 2027-08-28/30; 4) Kickoff bench 2027-08-29; 5) Redwood returns initial profile results 2027-09-02.
[08:52] Alicia: noted.
[08:54] Marcus: one last operational ask — include metrics for cost per 1k tokens and 99th percentile cost impact when scaling.
[08:59] Jordan: will do.
[09:01] Priya: ok I'll also include measurement detail: how we compute TTFT (server t_received to t_first_token), and TPOT (median inter-token delta, and p95/p99 of inter-token deltas), plus how we compute per-request tokens/sec and end-to-end client-observed time. We'll also note that streaming vs non-streaming changes numbers.
[09:22] Alicia: thanks all, this was helpful.
[09:24] Jordan: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.
[09:28] (meeting ends)
